notes.summary: Machine learning as function fitting from data: inputs, labels, loss, and the search for parameters. The Open Learning Library edition of MIT's 6.036 runs as a complete interactive course — reading, videos, and auto-graded exercises — which is why it's this curriculum's spine. This week builds the vocabulary every later lesson uses.
notes.focus: Write the 'ingredients' of an ML problem (data, hypothesis class, loss, optimizer) for spam classification. Framing precisely is half the job in practice.

notes.summary: The first model: a hyperplane separates classes. In 2D that's a line with weight vector theta and offset theta_0; signed distance decides class. Your 18.06 linear algebra returns immediately — dot products, norms, projections — the geometry of classification IS Strang's course applied.
notes.focus: For a given (theta, theta_0), classify 5 points by hand AND compute their margins. Geometry first — formulas follow.

notes.summary: How machines learn: define a smooth loss, compute its gradient, step downhill. Batch, mini-batch, and stochastic variants trade compute for noise; learning rate is the critical hyperparameter. This is the engine under every deep network you'll ever train — and every LLM you'll ever use.
notes.focus: Implement gradient descent for squared loss on 2 parameters and plot the trajectory on a contour plot. Seeing the zigzag cures learning-rate confusion.

notes.summary: Continuous outputs: squared loss, the normal equations, and the closed-form solution (X^T X)^-1 X^T y — pure 18.06. Polynomial features add expressiveness; regularization (ridge) tames it. You also meet the bias-variance trade-off formally: capacity vs data.
notes.focus: Fit a degree-9 polynomial to 10 noisy points, once plain and once ridge. Plot both — overfitting stops being a word and becomes a picture.

notes.summary: Probabilistic and margin-based classification: logistic regression squashes scores to probabilities and optimizes log loss; the perceptron and hinge-loss SVM maximize margins. All three are the same linear machine with different losses — a unification that makes 'which classifier' a design decision, not folklore.
notes.focus: Plot all three losses (squared, log, hinge) on one axis. One graph explains why SVMs care about the margin and logistic regression doesn't.

notes.summary: Nonlinear function approximation: layers of affine transforms with nonlinearities, trained by backpropagation — the chain rule organized as reverse-mode differentiation. You implement a small network from scratch here, which permanently demystifies the frameworks (PyTorch is this, industrialized).
notes.focus: Hand-compute backprop for a 2-layer network on ONE example with numbers. The arithmetic is tedious and the understanding is permanent.

notes.summary: Sequences: RNNs carry hidden state across time steps, trained by backpropagation through time. The reading adds the modern arc — attention and transformers as the sequence model that scaled to LLMs. Understanding the RNN baseline makes attention's advantages precise rather than fashionable.
notes.focus: Unroll a 4-step RNN by hand and count the gradient paths. Seeing the path lengths makes the vanishing-gradient problem — and attention's fix — obvious.

notes.summary: Beyond linear and neural: decision trees split feature space (interpretable!), kNN memorizes, and k-means clusters without labels (unsupervised). Feature engineering — the human work of representation — matters more for these models than architecture. This is classical ML: still the right first tool for tabular data.
concepts: kNN and the curse of dimensionality
notes.focus: Run k-means by hand on 8 points for 2 clusters, one full iteration. The geometric dance of centroids is the algorithm — nothing more.

notes.summary: The discipline that separates ML from curve fitting: train/validation/test splits, cross-validation, early stopping, and the model-selection protocol. Data leakage — the silent killer of real projects — gets explicit treatment. Every Kaggle disaster and production ML failure traces here.
notes.focus: Design the evaluation protocol for a time-series prediction task. The wrong split (random instead of temporal) leaks — find why before reading on.

lessons.title: Deep Learning Practice and Modern Architectures

notes.summary: The modern layer: convolutions for spatial structure, embeddings for categorical data, and the transformer architecture behind the current AI wave. Also the practical craft — batch norm, dropout, optimizers (Adam) — that makes deep nets trainable at all. This connects your 6.036 foundation to the systems in the news.
notes.focus: For a 28x28 image task, compare parameters: fully-connected layer vs conv 3x3. The 50x reduction is why vision went convolutional first.

notes.summary: High-dimensional data often hides in a low-dimensional subspace: PCA finds the directions of maximum variance via the SVD — your 18.06 training returning as a working tool. Eigenfaces (projecting face images onto principal components) is the classic demo, and dimensionality reduction becomes the bridge between raw features and every model you've trained.
notes.focus: Compute PCA of a small 2D dataset by hand (center, covariance, eigenvectors). Then project and reconstruct — the residual IS the information you threw away.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the classical core: geometry, gradient descent, regression, classifiers, and neural nets. Re-derive the gradient of log loss and the normal equations from a blank page — the derivations, memorized, are the exam. CS188 next door assumes this math is fluent.
notes.focus: Write the four losses (squared, log, hinge, perceptron) and their gradients side by side. One table, most of the course.

notes.summary: The close: end-to-end ML projects, fairness and bias in learned systems, and the full-course map from linear separators to transformers. Your artifact: a small end-to-end project (data cleaning through evaluation) in a notebook — the exact portfolio piece employers and CS188's ML lectures assume.
notes.focus: Ship that notebook project: clean data, trained model, honest validation, one-paragraph limitations. Honest ML is the whole discipline in miniature.
